meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do You Prefer Grass or Astroturf I Don't Know. I Never Smoked Astroturf'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mean Joe Greene. Quote Investigator traces the Astroturf quip to Mets pitcher Tug McGraw in 1974. Greene got the credit in a 1985 Scottish newspaper.

answer.label: Not Charles Edward Greene — actually Tug McGraw
answer.authorDates: 1944–2004 · Major League Baseball relief pitcher (Mets, Phillies)
answer.sourceLine: Mets reliever Tug McGraw told a reporter in April 1974 that a boy had phoned a San Francisco TV talk show to ask whether he preferred grass or astroturf, and “I told him that I had never smoked astroturf.” Quote Investigator ↗ documents this and concludes McGraw originated the quip. The credit to “Mean” Joe Greene comes from a 1985 Scottish newspaper.

source.heading: The earliest documented version

docMeta.dd: “McGraw: The Mets’ Wacky Folk Hero” by Garry Niver
The Times (San Mateo, California), April 30, 1974, page 19
Tug McGraw, then pitching for the New York Mets

source.excerpt: Back in the Mets’ locker room, McGraw laughed and said that he might get in trouble for something he said as a guest on a San Francisco TV talk show the day before. “A young boy called up and asked me if I preferred grass or astroturf,” chuckled Tug. “And I told him that I had never smoked astroturf. I guess that I shouldn’t have said that.”
trail: April 30, 1974 — The Times (San Mateo) runs an interview in which Tug McGraw says he “had never smoked astroturf,” a line he had given a caller on a TV talk show (Quote Investigator ↗).
June 30 and July 3, 1974 — The New York Times (“I don’t know, I’ve never smoked AstroTurf”) and then the Los Angeles Times print the quip, both crediting McGraw (Quote Investigator ↗).
1982 — Morrow’s International Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations credits Joe Namath instead (Quote Investigator ↗).
July 8, 1985 — Scotland’s Evening Times credits “big Mean Joe Green” (sic), in dialect: “Ah don’t know man. Ah ain’t ever smoked Astroturf” (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator. QI says it has not seen footage of the TV show, so McGraw’s exact words on air are not known. The short form people quote today, “I don’t know, I’ve never smoked AstroTurf,” appeared in the New York Times on June 30, 1974.

author.name: Tug McGraw
author.heading: About Tug McGraw
author.metaLine: 1944–2004 · MLB relief pitcher, New York Mets & Philadelphia Phillies
author.bio: Frank Edwin “Tug” McGraw Jr. pitched for the New York Mets (1965–1974) and the Philadelphia Phillies (1975–1984). He coined the Mets’ 1973 rallying cry “Ya Gotta Believe!” and got the final out of the Phillies’ 1980 World Series win. He was known as one of baseball’s great characters, and he was the father of country singer Tim McGraw.

copyAttribution: “I don’t know, I’ve never smoked AstroTurf.” — Tug McGraw, quoted in the New York Times, June 30, 1974; earliest documented in The Times (San Mateo), April 30, 1974. Often misattributed to “Mean” Joe Greene.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: After 1974 the quip was passed around and credited to several other famous athletes. Quote Investigator ↗ says these credits “appeared in later years and may be imitative and/or apocryphal.”

items.why: In July 1985, a Scottish Evening Times profile of a local American football team put the line in Greene’s mouth, in dialect. The paper spelled his name “Green.” QI cites nothing earlier that links Greene to the quip (Quote Investigator ↗).

Credited in Morrow’s International Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations (1982). Anthony Burgess repeated that credit in a 1986 collection, and quote websites such as iwise.com and thinkexist.com carried it as of 2011 (Quote Investigator ↗).
Paul Dickson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotations (2008) credits McGraw but notes that “this quote is also widely ascribed to Bill Lee” (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest record is McGraw’s own account in April 1974. QI concludes that “he originated this quip although it is possible that other athletes used it after he did” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the joke landed
lead: McGraw was known for offbeat sayings. He was the Mets reliever behind the 1973 rallying cry “Ya Gotta Believe!” (Wikipedia ↗). By his own account, he made the grass-versus-astroturf crack on live TV in answer to a young caller. He then told a reporter he might get in trouble for it.

The joke depends on the double meaning of “grass” as marijuana. A short version fits easily into a wisecrack column, which is how it reached the New York and Los Angeles papers within weeks. From there it drifted to bigger names in football, including Joe Namath and “Mean” Joe Greene.
context.pull: “I told him that I had never smoked astroturf.”
